content: Hygiene refers to practices that are essential for maintaining good health and cleanliness. Scientifically, the term hygiene encompasses the preservation of health and healthy living. It is commonly used in contexts such as personal hygiene, domestic hygiene, dental hygiene, and occupational hygiene, and is often associated with public health. The word hygiene originates from Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health, cleanliness, and sanitation. Hygiene is also a scientific discipline focused on promoting and preserving health, sometimes referred to as hygienics. Personal Hygiene Regular washing of the body and hair is essential to maintain cleanliness. Frequent washing of hands and face is critical to prevent the spread of germs. Oral hygiene involves caring for the teeth and gums, as well as addressing and preventing bad breath. This includes daily brushing with toothpaste and flossing to prevent tooth decay and gum disease. These practices also help manage and prevent halitosis (bad breath). Chewing gum or using antibacterial mouthwashes, such as Listerine, can further help eliminate bad breath. Cleaning clothes and living spaces regularly is necessary to maintain a hygienic environment. Avoid direct contact with bodily fluids, such as blood, feces, urine, and vomit, to prevent the transmission of infections. Avoid touching animals before eating, and wash hands thoroughly after handling animals and before meals. When coughing or sneezing, cover the mouth with a tissue or use the upper arm/elbow area instead of bare hands. If hands are used, wash them immediately afterward. Suppress unhygienic habits, such as nose-picking or touching pimples, to reduce the risk of infection. Avoid licking fingers before handling paper or turning pages in books. Instead, use rubber fingertip covers or glycerine-based products available at stationery stores. Refrain from biting fingernails, as this can introduce bacteria into the mouth. Wear clean underwear and clothing daily to maintain personal hygiene. Wash hands thoroughly after using the toilet to prevent the spread of germs. Avoid sharing personal items such as towels, combs, and hairbrushes to reduce the risk of cross-contamination. Change bed linens when a new person sleeps on the bed to ensure cleanliness. Food and Cooking Hygiene The primary goals of food and cooking hygiene are to prevent food contamination, reduce the transmission of diseases, and avoid food poisoning. Food hygiene protocols include cleaning food preparation areas and equipment, such as using separate cutting boards for raw meats and vegetables. Sterilization may involve the use of chlorine bleach. Avoid consuming meats contaminated with pathogens like trichina worms or salmonella. Thoroughly cook questionable meats to ensure safety. Exercise caution when preparing raw foods, such as sushi and sashimi, to minimize the risk of contamination. Institutional dish sanitization involves washing with soap and clean water to ensure proper hygiene. Wash hands after handling uncooked food during meal preparation to prevent cross-contamination. Use separate utensils for preparing different types of food to avoid cross-contamination. Avoid sharing cutlery while eating to reduce the risk of spreading germs. Refrain from licking fingers or hands during or after eating. Do not reuse serving utensils that have been licked or contaminated. Store food properly to prevent contamination by pests or vermin. Refrigerate perishable foods and avoid storing certain foods in environments where refrigeration is not feasible. Label food with production dates or best before dates to ensure safe consumption. Dispose of uneaten food and packaging properly to maintain cleanliness. Medical Hygiene Properly bandage and dress injuries to prevent infection. Use protective clothing, such as masks, gowns, caps, eyewear, and gloves, to reduce the risk of contamination during medical procedures. Sterilize surgical instruments to ensure they are free from pathogens. Dispose of medical waste safely to prevent the spread of infectious diseases. Many of these practices were developed in the 19th century and became well-established by the mid-20th century. Some procedures, such as medical waste disposal, were further refined in response to late 20th-century disease outbreaks, including AIDS and Ebola. Personal Service Hygiene Instruments used by hairdressers should be sterilized to prevent the spread of infections. Tools used in body piercing and tattooing should be sterilized using an autoclave to ensure safety. In food outlets, individuals should clean their hands before eating, either by washing with soap or using wet wipes. Historical Hygiene Practices Elaborate hygiene codes can be found in ancient Hindu texts, such as the Manusmriti and the Vishnu Purana. Bathing is one of the five Nitya Karmas (daily duties) in Sikhism, and neglecting it is considered sinful in some scriptures. These codes were based on ritual purity rather than an understanding of disease transmission, though some practices inadvertently improved hygiene from an epidemiological perspective. Regular bathing was a hallmark of Roman civilization. Urban areas featured elaborate public baths with large pools, smaller hot and cold pools, saunas, and spa-like facilities for depilation, oiling, and massage. Water was continuously replenished via aqueduct-fed systems. Outside urban centers, smaller bathing facilities or clean natural water sources were used. Roman cities also had large sewer systems, such as Rome's Cloaca Maxima, which drained public and private latrines. While Romans did not have demand-flush toilets, some toilets featured a continuous flow of water beneath them. Until the late 19th century, indoor facilities for bodily functions were typically limited to the elite in Western cities. The majority of the population relied on communal facilities built over cesspools. This changed after Dr. John Snow discovered that cholera was transmitted through fecal contamination of water. Although his findings were initially met with resistance, governments and sanitary reformers eventually recognized the health benefits of sewer systems, leading to the widespread adoption of flush toilets and the moral imperative for private, indoor bathrooms. European Hygiene Practices Contrary to popular belief, bathing and sanitation were not abandoned in Europe after the fall of the Roman Empire. Soapmaking became an established trade during the so-called Dark Ages. The Romans primarily used scented oils, often imported from Egypt, as alternatives to soap. The myth that chamber pots were emptied into streets during the European Middle Ages is inaccurate; this was a Roman practice. Bathing remained common in Europe until shortly after the Renaissance, when it was replaced by sweat-bathing and heavy use of perfumes. This shift was due to the belief that water could transmit disease through the skin. While water can carry disease, it is more likely to do so when consumed rather than through bathing, and only if contaminated by pathogens. Modern sanitation practices were not widely adopted until the 19th and 20th centuries. According to medieval historian Lynn Thorndike, people in Medieval Europe likely bathed more frequently than Westerners did in the 19th century. Grooming Personal grooming refers to enhancing one’s physical appearance or appeal by addressing visible imperfections or improving hygiene. Grooming activities typically include washing and cleaning the hair, combing to remove tangles, and styling. It may also involve cosmetic care, such as shaving or other forms of depilation.
